solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Enzymes isolated from organisms living at very high temperatures, as in hot vents and sulphur springs, retain their catalytic power even at 80–90 °C.
Reason (R): Each enzyme shows its highest activity at a particular temperature and pH called the optimum temperature and optimum pH.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT states both: enzymes from organisms of extremely hot habitats are stable and keep their catalytic power at 80–90 °C, and every enzyme has an optimum temperature and pH. R is a general property of all enzymes; it does not explain why these particular enzymes are thermally stable.
steps: A: thermostable enzymes from hot vents → true
R: optimum temperature and pH → true
General property ≠ cause of thermal stability → R does not explain A
solution.why_others_wrong: Option A treats a general property as the cause; C and D call a true statement false.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Biomolecules', enzymes: nature of enzyme action; factors affecting enzyme activity
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about proteins are correct?

(a) Proteins are heteropolymers of amino acids.
(b) The first amino acid of a polypeptide is called the C-terminal amino acid.
(c) Insulin is a protein that acts as a hormone.
(d) The three-dimensional tertiary structure of a protein is necessary for many of its biological activities.
(e) The secondary structure of a protein is the sequence of amino acids in it.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Proteins are linear chains of amino acids, i.e. heteropolymers. The first amino acid of a chain is the N-terminal amino acid and the last is the C-terminal. NCERT's table lists insulin as a hormone. The tertiary structure is absolutely necessary for many biological activities. The sequence of amino acids is the primary structure, not the secondary.
solution.why_others_wrong: A and C include (b); D includes (e).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Biomolecules', proteins; structure of proteins

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: As substrate concentration is raised, the velocity of an enzyme-catalysed reaction rises at first and then reaches a maximum (Vmax) that is not exceeded by any further rise in substrate concentration. This is because:

options.text: The enzyme molecules are fewer than the substrate molecules, and after they are saturated no free enzyme molecules are left to bind the extra substrate
The extra substrate denatures the enzyme
The extra substrate acts as a competitive inhibitor
The products formed lower the activation energy further

solution.explanation: NCERT: the velocity rises with substrate concentration and reaches Vmax, which is not exceeded, because the enzyme molecules are fewer than the substrate molecules; once they are all saturated, there are no free enzyme molecules to bind more substrate.
steps: All enzyme molecules occupied → saturation → Vmax
solution.why_others_wrong: Substrate does not denature the enzyme or act as its own competitive inhibitor; products do not lower the activation energy.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Biomolecules', enzymes: factors affecting enzyme activity
solution.final_answer: Option A: The enzyme molecules are fewer than the substrate molecules, and after they are saturated no free enzyme molecules are left to bind the extra substrate

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Almost all enzymes are proteins.
Statement II: Like inorganic catalysts, enzymes work efficiently at high temperatures and high pressures.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: Almost all enzymes are proteins; a few nucleic acids also act as enzymes (Statement I true). Inorganic catalysts work efficiently at high temperatures and pressures, whereas enzymes get damaged at high temperatures (say above 40 °C) (Statement II false).
steps: Almost all enzymes are proteins → I true
Enzymes are damaged above about 40 °C → II false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Biomolecules', enzymes
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Essential amino acids have to be supplied through our diet.
Reason (R): Our body cannot make essential amino acids, whereas it can make the non-essential ones.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: Dietary proteins are the source of essential amino acids. Non-essential amino acids are those our body can make; essential ones it cannot make, so they must come from food. R is exactly why A is true.
steps: A: essential amino acids from diet → true
R: body cannot synthesise them → true
solution.why_others_wrong: B denies the direct causal link; C and D call a true statement false.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Biomolecules', proteins
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: A protein is made of two polypeptide chains, one of 21 amino acids and the other of 30 amino acids. Each chain is a linear chain of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. How many peptide bonds are present in the protein?

solution.explanation: In a linear chain of n amino acids, n − 1 peptide bonds join neighbours. Each chain is counted separately because there is no peptide bond between the two chains.
solution.shortcut: Peptide bonds = total amino acids − number of chains = 51 − 2 = 49.
solution.why_others_wrong: 51 counts amino acids, not bonds; 50 treats both chains as one continuous chain; 48 subtracts one bond too many.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Biomolecules', proteins

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) Proteins, nucleic acids and polysaccharides are found in the acid-insoluble fraction of a living tissue.
(b) Biomolecules of the acid-insoluble fraction other than lipids have molecular weights of ten thousand daltons and above.
(c) A nucleic acid containing deoxyribose is DNA, while one containing ribose is RNA.
(d) In a protein, adjacent amino acids are joined by glycosidic bonds.
(e) The sugar found in polynucleotides is a hexose.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Grinding a tissue in trichloroacetic acid gives an acid-insoluble fraction of proteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides and lipids. Except lipids, these have molecular weights of ten thousand daltons and above. The sugar of polynucleotides is ribose or 2'-deoxyribose, both pentoses; deoxyribose gives DNA and ribose RNA. Amino acids in proteins are linked by peptide bonds; glycosidic bonds link sugars.
solution.why_others_wrong: A includes (e); B and D include (d).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Biomolecules', biomacromolecules; nucleic acids

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (lipid) with List-II (feature).

List-I:
A. Palmitic acid
B. Arachidonic acid
C. Lecithin
D. Gingelly oil

List-II:
I. Phospholipid found in cell membranes
II. Fatty acid with 20 carbon atoms including the carboxyl carbon
III. Fatty acid with 16 carbon atoms including the carboxyl carbon
IV. Has a low melting point and remains liquid in winter

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Palmitic acid has 16 carbons and arachidonic acid 20 carbons, each count including the carboxyl carbon. Lecithin is a phospholipid found in cell membranes. Oils such as gingelly oil have lower melting points and stay liquid in winter.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap the two fatty acids, or lecithin with the oil, or lecithin with palmitic acid.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Biomolecules', analysis of chemical composition: lipids
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: Which sequence correctly describes the catalytic cycle of an enzyme?

options.text: Products are released → substrate binds to the active site → bonds of the substrate are broken → enzyme alters its shape
Enzyme alters its shape → substrate binds to a site away from the active site → products are released → enzyme–product complex forms
Substrate binds to the active site → bonds of the substrate are broken → enzyme alters its shape around the products → products stay bound permanently

Substrate binds to the active site → enzyme alters its shape to fit more tightly around the substrate → bonds of the substrate are broken and an enzyme–product complex forms → products are released and the free enzyme can bind another substrate molecule

solution.explanation: NCERT gives four steps: (1) the substrate binds to the active site; (2) binding induces the enzyme to alter its shape and fit more tightly around the substrate; (3) the active site breaks the chemical bonds of the substrate and an enzyme–product complex forms; (4) the enzyme releases the products and the free enzyme is ready for another substrate molecule.
steps: Bind → induced fit → bond breaking (EP complex) → release and reuse
solution.why_others_wrong: A and B scramble the order (release before binding, binding away from the active site); C keeps the products bound, but the enzyme is released unchanged for reuse.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Biomolecules', enzymes: nature of enzyme action
solution.final_answer: Option D: Substrate binds to the active site → enzyme alters its shape to fit more tightly around the substrate → bonds of the substrate are broken and an enzyme–product complex forms → products are released and the free enzyme can bind another substrate molecule

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: Which statement about the classification and naming of enzymes is correct?

options.text: Enzymes are divided into 6 classes, each with 4–13 subclasses, and each enzyme is named by a four-digit number
Enzymes are divided into 4 classes, each with 6–13 subclasses, and each enzyme is named by a six-digit number
Enzymes are divided into 13 classes, each with 4–6 subclasses, and each enzyme is named by a four-letter code
Enzymes are divided into 6 classes, each with exactly 4 subclasses, and each enzyme is named by a two-digit number

solution.explanation: NCERT: enzymes are divided into 6 classes (oxidoreductases/dehydrogenases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases and ligases), each with 4–13 subclasses, and are named accordingly by a four-digit number.
solution.why_others_wrong: B, C and D change the number of classes, the number of subclasses or the length of the code.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Biomolecules', enzymes: classification and nomenclature of enzymes
solution.final_answer: Option A: Enzymes are divided into 6 classes, each with 4–13 subclasses, and each enzyme is named by a four-digit number

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: The cartilaginous box of the human respiratory tract that helps in sound production, and is therefore called the sound box, is the:

solution.explanation: The pharynx opens through the larynx into the trachea. The larynx is a cartilaginous box that helps in sound production and is hence called the sound box.
steps: Nostrils → nasal chamber → pharynx → larynx (sound box) → trachea
solution.why_others_wrong: The pharynx is a common passage for food and air; the trachea and bronchioles are air tubes, not the sound box.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Breathing and Exchange of Gases', human respiratory system

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: During swallowing, the entry of food into the larynx is prevented by a thin, elastic, cartilaginous flap called the:

solution.explanation: During swallowing, the glottis can be covered by a thin elastic cartilaginous flap called the epiglottis, which prevents the entry of food into the larynx.
steps: Epiglottis covers the glottis during swallowing
solution.why_others_wrong: The glottis is the opening that gets covered; the pleura covers the lungs; the diaphragm separates thorax from abdomen.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Breathing and Exchange of Gases', human respiratory system

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: The lungs are covered by a double-layered pleura with pleural fluid between the layers. The pleural fluid:

options.text: Reduces friction on the lung surface
Forms the exchange surface of the alveoli

solution.explanation: The lungs are covered by a double-layered pleura with pleural fluid between the layers, which reduces friction on the lung surface. The outer pleural membrane is in close contact with the thoracic lining and the inner one with the lung surface.
solution.why_others_wrong: NCERT gives only one role for pleural fluid, reducing friction; gas exchange takes place across the alveolar wall, not through the pleura.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Breathing and Exchange of Gases', human respiratory system
solution.final_answer: Option A: Reduces friction on the lung surface

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: A healthy man has a tidal volume of 500 mL, an expiratory reserve volume of 1100 mL and an inspiratory reserve volume of 3000 mL, and he breathes 14 times per minute at rest. What volume of air does he inspire per minute during normal breathing?

solution.explanation: During normal breathing, the volume inspired in each breath is the tidal volume. Volume per minute = tidal volume × breathing rate. NCERT notes that a healthy man can inspire or expire about 6000 to 8000 mL of air per minute; 7000 mL lies in that range. The reserve volumes are used only in forcible breathing.
solution.why_others_wrong: 35.7 mL divides instead of multiplying; 514 mL adds the rate to the volume; 22,400 mL wrongly adds the ERV to each breath.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Breathing and Exchange of Gases', respiratory volumes and capacities

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (animal) with List-II (respiratory surface).

List-I:
A. Flatworms
B. Earthworms
C. Fishes
D. Frogs

List-II:
I. Gills
II. Lungs and moist skin
III. Simple diffusion over the entire body surface
IV. Moist cuticle

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Lower invertebrates such as sponges, coelenterates and flatworms exchange gases by simple diffusion over the entire body surface. Earthworms use their moist cuticle. Fishes use gills. Amphibians such as frogs respire through lungs and can also respire through their moist skin.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap flatworms with earthworms, fishes with frogs, or earthworms with fishes.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Breathing and Exchange of Gases', respiratory organs
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Contraction of the diaphragm increases the volume of the thoracic chamber in the antero-posterior axis.
Reason (R): Contraction of the external inter-costal muscles lifts up the ribs and the sternum, increasing the volume of the thoracic chamber in the dorso-ventral axis.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: Both statements are NCERT facts about inspiration. A concerns the diaphragm (antero-posterior axis); R concerns a different set of muscles, the external inter-costals (dorso-ventral axis). R describes a separate contribution to the rise in thoracic volume and does not explain A.
steps: R: external inter-costals → dorso-ventral axis → true
Different muscles, different axes → R does not explain A
solution.why_others_wrong: A treats an independent muscle action as the cause; C and D call a true statement false.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Breathing and Exchange of Gases', mechanism of breathing
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Which of the following definitions of respiratory volumes and capacities are correct?

(a) Residual volume is the volume of air remaining in the lungs even after a forcible expiration.
(b) Vital capacity is the maximum volume of air a person can breathe in after a forced expiration.
(c) Functional residual capacity is the expiratory reserve volume plus the residual volume.
(d) Inspiratory capacity is the tidal volume plus the expiratory reserve volume.
(e) Total lung capacity is the vital capacity plus the residual volume.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: RV is the air left after forcible expiration. VC (ERV + TV + IRV) is the maximum volume breathed in after a forced expiration (or out after a forced inspiration). FRC = ERV + RV. Inspiratory capacity is TV + IRV, not TV + ERV (that sum is the expiratory capacity). TLC = VC + RV.
solution.why_others_wrong: B, C and D include the false statement (d); B and C also leave out true statements.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Breathing and Exchange of Gases', respiratory volumes and capacities

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The diffusion membrane is made of three major layers: the thin squamous epithelium of the alveoli, the endothelium of the alveolar capillaries, and the basement substance between them.
Statement II: The total thickness of the diffusion membrane is much more than a millimetre.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: The diffusion membrane has three major layers: alveolar squamous epithelium, capillary endothelium and the basement substance between them (Statement I true). Its total thickness is much less than a millimetre, which favours diffusion (Statement II false).
steps: Thickness much less than 1 mm → II false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Breathing and Exchange of Gases', exchange of gases
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: Which set of conditions, found in the alveoli, favours the formation of oxyhaemoglobin?

options.text: Low pO₂, high pCO₂, higher H⁺ concentration and higher temperature
High pO₂, high pCO₂, higher H⁺ concentration and lower temperature
Low pO₂, low pCO₂, lesser H⁺ concentration and higher temperature
High pO₂, low pCO₂, lesser H⁺ concentration and lower temperature

solution.explanation: Binding of O₂ to haemoglobin depends mainly on pO₂; pCO₂, H⁺ concentration and temperature also interfere. In the alveoli there is high pO₂, low pCO₂, lesser H⁺ concentration and lower temperature, all favourable for oxyhaemoglobin formation. The opposite conditions in the tissues favour dissociation of O₂.
solution.why_others_wrong: A gives the tissue conditions, which favour dissociation; B and C mix favourable and unfavourable factors.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Breathing and Exchange of Gases', transport of gases: transport of oxygen
solution.final_answer: Option D: High pO₂, low pCO₂, lesser H⁺ concentration and lower temperature

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: The partial pressures (in mm Hg) are: alveoli, pO₂ 104 and pCO₂ 40; deoxygenated blood, pO₂ 40 and pCO₂ 45; oxygenated blood, pO₂ 95 and pCO₂ 40. What are the partial-pressure gradients for O₂ from the alveoli to the deoxygenated blood reaching the lungs, and for CO₂ from that blood to the alveoli?

options.text: 55 mm Hg for O₂ and 5 mm Hg for CO₂
64 mm Hg for O₂ and 5 mm Hg for CO₂
64 mm Hg for O₂ and 45 mm Hg for CO₂
104 mm Hg for O₂ and 40 mm Hg for CO₂

solution.explanation: Gas moves down its partial-pressure gradient. Deoxygenated blood arrives at the alveoli, so the O₂ gradient is alveolar pO₂ minus blood pO₂, and the CO₂ gradient is blood pCO₂ minus alveolar pCO₂.
steps: CO₂ still diffuses readily because its solubility is 20–25 times that of O₂
solution.why_others_wrong: 55 mm Hg uses the oxygenated-blood pO₂ (95) in place of the alveolar value; 45 mm Hg is the blood pCO₂ itself, not a difference; 104 and 40 are the alveolar values, not gradients.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Breathing and Exchange of Gases', exchange of gases
solution.final_answer: Option B: 64 mm Hg for O₂ and 5 mm Hg for CO₂

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): RBCs contain a very high concentration of the enzyme carbonic anhydrase, and minute quantities of it are present in the plasma too.
Reason (R): At the alveolar site, where pCO₂ is high, carbonic anhydrase converts CO₂ and water into HCO₃⁻ and H⁺.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: A is an NCERT statement. At the tissue site, where pCO₂ is high because of catabolism, CO₂ diffuses into blood and forms HCO₃⁻ and H⁺. At the alveolar site pCO₂ is low, and the reaction runs the opposite way, releasing CO₂ and H₂O. R puts the high pCO₂ at the alveoli and the forward reaction there, so R is false.
steps: A: high carbonic anhydrase in RBCs, minute amount in plasma → true
Alveoli: low pCO₂ → HCO₃⁻ → CO₂ + H₂O → R false
solution.why_others_wrong: A and B need R to be true; D calls the true assertion false.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Breathing and Exchange of Gases', transport of gases: transport of carbon dioxide
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about respiratory disorders are correct?

(a) Cigarette smoking is one of the major causes of emphysema.
(b) Long exposure to the dust of grinding or stone-breaking industries can cause inflammation leading to fibrosis and serious lung damage.
(c) Workers in such industries should wear protective masks.
(d) In grinding and stone-breaking industries, the body's defence mechanism can fully cope with the dust produced.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT: cigarette smoking is one of the major causes of emphysema. In industries involving grinding or stone-breaking, so much dust is produced that the body's defence mechanism cannot fully cope; long exposure causes inflammation, fibrosis (proliferation of fibrous tissue) and serious lung damage, so workers should wear protective masks.
steps: (d) False: the defence mechanism cannot fully cope
solution.why_others_wrong: A leaves out (c); B and C include the false statement (d).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Breathing and Exchange of Gases', disorders of respiratory system

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: Which sequence correctly describes normal (quiet) expiration in humans?

options.text: Diaphragm and inter-costal muscles relax → diaphragm and sternum return to their normal positions → thoracic and pulmonary volumes decrease → intra-pulmonary pressure rises slightly above atmospheric pressure → air is expelled
Diaphragm and external inter-costal muscles contract → thoracic volume increases → intra-pulmonary pressure rises above atmospheric pressure → air is expelled
Diaphragm relaxes → thoracic volume increases → intra-pulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric pressure → air is expelled
Inter-costal muscles relax → pulmonary volume increases → intra-pulmonary pressure becomes equal to atmospheric pressure → air is expelled

solution.explanation: Relaxation of the diaphragm and the inter-costal muscles returns the diaphragm and sternum to their normal positions and reduces the thoracic volume and thereby the pulmonary volume. Intra-pulmonary pressure rises to slightly above atmospheric pressure, and air is expelled.
steps: Volume falls → pressure rises above atmospheric
solution.why_others_wrong: B describes the muscle action of inspiration; C and D let volume rise during expiration, and air cannot flow out when the inside pressure is lower than or equal to the outside pressure.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Breathing and Exchange of Gases', mechanism of breathing
solution.final_answer: Option A: Diaphragm and inter-costal muscles relax → diaphragm and sternum return to their normal positions → thoracic and pulmonary volumes decrease → intra-pulmonary pressure rises slightly above atmospheric pressure → air is expelled

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: A healthy adult human has, on average, how much haemoglobin in every 100 mL of blood?

solution.explanation: RBCs contain the red, iron-containing protein haemoglobin. A healthy individual has 12–16 g of haemoglobin in every 100 mL of blood.
steps: Haemoglobin → 12–16 g per 100 mL of blood
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.2–1.6 g and 120–160 g are off by a factor of ten; 5–5.5 is the RBC count in millions per mm³, not grams of haemoglobin.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Body Fluids and Circulation', blood: formed elements

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: RBCs have an average life span of 120 days, after which they are destroyed in the organ called the 'graveyard of RBCs'. This organ is the:

solution.explanation: RBCs live on average 120 days and are then destroyed in the spleen, the graveyard of RBCs. In adults they are formed in the red bone marrow.
solution.why_others_wrong: Red bone marrow is where RBCs are formed; NCERT names the spleen, not the liver or kidney, as the graveyard of RBCs.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Body Fluids and Circulation', blood: formed elements

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: Which plasma proteins are primarily involved in the defence mechanisms of the body?

solution.explanation: Fibrinogen, globulins and albumins are the major plasma proteins. Fibrinogens are needed for clotting, globulins are primarily involved in defence mechanisms, and albumins help in osmotic balance.
solution.why_others_wrong: Albumins maintain osmotic balance; fibrinogens act in clotting; haemoglobin is inside RBCs, not a plasma protein.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Body Fluids and Circulation', blood: plasma

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: The heart rate of a person can be found by counting the QRS complexes in an ECG over a known time. If 18 QRS complexes are recorded in 15 seconds, the heart rate is:

solution.explanation: Each QRS complex marks one depolarisation of the ventricles, i.e. one heartbeat. NCERT notes that counting QRS complexes in a given time gives the heart rate.
solution.why_others_wrong: 50 per minute inverts the ratio (15 × 60 / 18); 270 multiplies 18 by 15; 36 scales 15 s up to 30 s only.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Body Fluids and Circulation', electrocardiograph (ECG)

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: The heart of fishes has:

options.text: Three chambers: two atria and one ventricle
Four chambers: two atria and two ventricles
Three chambers: one atrium and two ventricles
Two chambers: an atrium and a ventricle

solution.explanation: Fishes have a two-chambered heart with an atrium and a ventricle. Amphibians and reptiles (except crocodiles) have a three-chambered heart with two atria and one ventricle; crocodiles, birds and mammals have a four-chambered heart. In fishes the heart pumps out deoxygenated blood, which is oxygenated by the gills.
solution.why_others_wrong: A is the amphibian heart, B the bird and mammal heart; C does not occur in vertebrates.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Body Fluids and Circulation', circulatory pathways
solution.final_answer: Option D: Two chambers: an atrium and a ventricle

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Lymph is a colourless fluid containing specialised lymphocytes, which are responsible for the immune responses of the body.
Statement II: Fats are absorbed through lymph in the lacteals present in the intestinal villi.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: Lymph is a colourless fluid with specialised lymphocytes responsible for immune responses; it is also an important carrier of nutrients and hormones. Fats are absorbed through lymph in the lacteals of the intestinal villi. Both statements are true.
steps: Fat absorption via lacteals → II true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Body Fluids and Circulation', lymph (tissue fluid)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (component of blood) with List-II (normal value).

List-I:
A. Erythrocytes
B. Leucocytes
C. Platelets
D. Plasma

List-II:
I. 6000–8000 per mm³ of blood
II. About 55 per cent of blood
III. 1,50,000–3,50,000 per mm³ of blood
IV. 5–5.5 million per mm³ of blood

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: A healthy adult has 5–5.5 million RBCs, 6000–8000 WBCs and 1,50,000–3,50,000 platelets per mm³ of blood. Plasma forms nearly 55 per cent of the blood; formed elements form about 45 per cent.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap WBC and platelet counts, RBC and WBC counts, or platelets with plasma.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Body Fluids and Circulation', blood: plasma and formed elements
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-IV, B-I, C-III, D-II

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The human heart is called myogenic.
Reason (R): The normal activities of the heart are regulated intrinsically (auto-regulated) by specialised muscles, the nodal tissue.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: normal activities of the heart are regulated intrinsically, i.e. auto-regulated by specialised muscles (nodal tissue); hence the heart is called myogenic. R is the reason for the term in A.
steps: R: auto-regulated by nodal tissue → true
'Hence' links R to A → R explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: B denies the link NCERT states with 'hence'; C and D call a true statement false.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Body Fluids and Circulation', regulation of cardiac activity

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the formed elements of blood are correct?

(a) In adults, RBCs are formed in the red bone marrow.
(b) In most mammals, RBCs are nucleated and spherical.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: RBCs are formed in the red bone marrow in adults; in most mammals they lack a nucleus and are biconcave. Platelets (thrombocytes) are cell fragments from megakaryocytes, and a fall in their number causes clotting disorders with excessive blood loss. Erythrocytes are the most abundant cells in blood.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: In human double circulation, the pulmonary artery carries:

options.text: Oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the body
Deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs
Oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium
Deoxygenated blood from the body to the right atrium

solution.explanation: Deoxygenated blood pumped by the right ventricle enters the pulmonary artery and goes to the lungs. Oxygenated blood returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium. This is the pulmonary circulation.

Statement II: The walls of the ventricles are much thinner than the walls of the atria.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the cardiac cycle are correct?

(a) As the ventricles contract, ventricular pressure rises and closes the tricuspid and bicuspid valves because of the attempted backflow of blood into the atria.
(b) As ventricular pressure rises further, the semilunar valves guarding the pulmonary artery and the aorta are forced open.
(c) As the ventricles relax, ventricular pressure falls and the semilunar valves close, preventing backflow.
(d) Each ventricle pumps out about 70 mL of blood in each cardiac cycle.
(e) The atria and the ventricles contract at the same time.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: During ventricular systole the rising pressure first closes the atrio-ventricular valves and then forces the semilunar valves open. When the ventricles relax, their pressure falls and the semilunar valves close. The stroke volume is about 70 mL per ventricle per cycle. The atria contract first (atrial systole) and the ventricles afterwards, when the action potential reaches them through the AVN and bundle of His; the two do not contract together.
steps: (e) False: atrial systole precedes ventricular systole
solution.why_others_wrong: A and D include (e); C leaves out the true statement (a).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Body Fluids and Circulation', cardiac cycle

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Neural signals through the sympathetic nerves decrease the rate of heartbeat.
Reason (R): Adrenal medullary hormones can increase the cardiac output.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: Sympathetic signals increase the rate of heartbeat, the strength of ventricular contraction and thereby the cardiac output; it is parasympathetic signals that decrease them. So A is false. Adrenal medullary hormones can also increase the cardiac output, so R is true.
steps: A: sympathetic → increases heart rate → A false
R: adrenal medullary hormones ↑ cardiac output → true
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and C all require the assertion to be true.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Body Fluids and Circulation', regulation of cardiac activity
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:

List-I:
A. Neutrophils
B. Eosinophils
C. Basophils
D. Lymphocytes

List-II:
I. 0.5–1
II. 20–25
III. 60–65
IV. 2–3

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Neutrophils are the most abundant WBCs (60–65 per cent) and basophils the least (0.5–1 per cent). Eosinophils form 2–3 per cent and lymphocytes 20–25 per cent (monocytes 6–8 per cent).

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: A person with blood group B needs a transfusion. Which option lists all the ABO donor groups whose blood is compatible with this person?

solution.explanation: A group B person has antigen B on the RBCs and anti-A antibodies in plasma. Donor RBCs must therefore not carry antigen A. Group B (antigen B) and group O (no antigens) qualify; A and AB carry antigen A.
steps: Donor RBCs must lack antigen A
solution.why_others_wrong: AB and A donor cells carry antigen A, which the recipient's anti-A would attack; 'B only' leaves out group O, which is also compatible.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: As blood passes through the capillaries in tissues, some fluid moves out into the spaces between the cells. Which statement about this interstitial (tissue) fluid is correct?

options.text: It contains all the formed elements of blood but no water-soluble substances
It contains the larger plasma proteins but no minerals
It has the same mineral distribution as plasma, while the larger proteins and most formed elements stay in the blood vessels
It is identical to plasma, including the larger proteins

solution.explanation: Water and many small water-soluble substances move out of the capillaries, leaving the larger proteins and most formed elements in the blood vessels. This interstitial fluid has the same mineral distribution as plasma. Exchange of nutrients and gases between blood and cells always occurs through it.
steps: Large proteins + most formed elements stay behind
solution.why_others_wrong: Formed elements and larger proteins mostly stay in the vessels, so A, B and D are wrong; minerals do pass out, which also rules out B.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Body Fluids and Circulation', lymph (tissue fluid)
solution.final_answer: Option C: It has the same mineral distribution as plasma, while the larger proteins and most formed elements stay in the blood vessels

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: Which of the following groups includes many ammonotelic animals?

solution.explanation: Ammonia is the most toxic nitrogenous waste and needs much water for its removal. Many bony fishes, aquatic amphibians and aquatic insects are ammonotelic; ammonia diffuses out across body surfaces or gill surfaces as ammonium ions.
steps: Ammonotelic → many bony fishes, aquatic amphibians, aquatic insects
solution.why_others_wrong: Mammals are ureotelic; birds and land snails are uricotelic.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Excretory Products and their Elimination', introduction: ammonotelism, ureotelism, uricotelism

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: The renal tubule of a nephron begins with a double-walled, cup-like structure that encloses the glomerulus. This structure is the:

solution.explanation: Each nephron has a glomerulus and a renal tubule. The tubule begins with the double-walled, cup-like Bowman's capsule, which encloses the glomerulus; together they form the Malpighian body (renal corpuscle).
steps: Then PCT → Henle's loop → DCT → collecting duct
solution.why_others_wrong: Henle's loop and the collecting duct are later parts of the tubule; the renal pelvis is a funnel-shaped space of the kidney, not part of a nephron.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Excretory Products and their Elimination', human excretory system: nephron

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Urine formed by the nephrons is stored in the urinary bladder until a voluntary signal is given by the central nervous system.
Statement II: During micturition, the smooth muscles of the bladder relax and the urethral sphincter contracts.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: Urine is stored in the bladder until the CNS gives a voluntary signal (Statement I true). When the bladder fills, stretch receptors send signals to the CNS, which sends motor messages that contract the smooth muscles of the bladder and simultaneously relax the urethral sphincter, releasing urine (Statement II false).
steps: Storage until voluntary CNS signal → I true
Bladder muscles contract, sphincter relaxes → II false
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Excretory Products and their Elimination', micturition
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: Filtrate enters the descending limb of Henle's loop at an osmolarity of 300 mOsmol L⁻¹ and reaches the hairpin bend at 1200 mOsmol L⁻¹. Assume that the amount of solute in the filtrate does not change along this limb. If 20 mL of filtrate enters the descending limb, what volume reaches the hairpin bend?

solution.concept: Concentration of the filtrate in the descending limb
solution.explanation: NCERT: the descending limb of the loop of Henle is permeable to water but almost impermeable to electrolytes, so the filtrate gets concentrated as it moves down by losing water, while its solutes stay in it. With the solute amount fixed, volume × osmolarity stays constant, so a four-fold rise in osmolarity means the volume falls to one-fourth.
solution.shortcut: Osmolarity rises 4-fold (300 → 1200), so the volume falls to 1/4 of 20 mL.
solution.why_others_wrong: 80 mL multiplies by the ratio instead of dividing; 15 mL is the volume of water lost, not the volume left; 20 mL assumes the filtrate is concentrated by gaining solutes, but this limb is almost impermeable to electrolytes.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Excretory Products and their Elimination', urine formation: function of the tubules (Henle's loop) and mechanism of concentration of the filtrate

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Our lungs remove large amounts of CO₂ (about 200 mL per minute) and also significant quantities of water every day.
Reason (R): The liver secretes bile containing substances such as bilirubin, biliverdin, cholesterol, degraded steroid hormones, vitamins and drugs.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Role of other organs in excretion
solution.explanation: Both are NCERT examples of organs other than the kidneys that help in excretion: the lungs remove CO₂ and water, and the liver eliminates substances through bile. The liver's bile has no bearing on what the lungs remove, so R does not explain A.
steps: A: lungs remove ~200 mL CO₂ per minute and water → true
Two separate organs and processes → R does not explain A
solution.why_others_wrong: A links two unrelated facts; C and D call a true statement false.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Excretory Products and their Elimination', role of other organs in excretion
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the functions of the renal tubule are correct?

(a) The PCT is lined by simple cuboidal brush border epithelium, which increases the surface area for reabsorption.
(b) The PCT helps to maintain the pH and ionic balance of body fluids by selective secretion of H⁺, ammonia and K⁺ into the filtrate and absorption of HCO₃⁻ from it.
(c) Reabsorption in Henle's loop is the maximum of all segments of the tubule.
(d) The collecting duct helps to maintain the pH and ionic balance of blood by selective secretion of H⁺ and K⁺.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: The brush border of the PCT increases the surface for reabsorption, and the PCT secretes H⁺, NH₃ and K⁺ and absorbs HCO₃⁻. Reabsorption in Henle's loop is minimum; this region instead maintains the high osmolarity of the medullary interstitial fluid. The collecting duct also secretes H⁺ and K⁺ selectively.
steps: (c) False: reabsorption in Henle's loop is minimum
solution.why_others_wrong: A leaves out (b) and (d) and includes (c); B and C include the false statement (c).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Excretory Products and their Elimination', function of the tubules

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: Which of the following is reabsorbed from the glomerular filtrate by active transport?

options.text: Water in the initial segments of the nephron

solution.explanation: Substances such as glucose, amino acids and Na⁺ are reabsorbed actively. Nitrogenous wastes are absorbed by passive transport, and water is reabsorbed passively in the initial segments of the nephron.
steps: Passive → nitrogenous wastes; water in initial segments
solution.why_others_wrong: Nitrogenous wastes and water move passively; ammonia is secreted into the filtrate, not reabsorbed.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Excretory Products and their Elimination', urine formation: reabsorption

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (blood vessel) with List-II (description).

List-I:
A. Afferent arteriole
B. Efferent arteriole
C. Peritubular capillaries
D. Vasa recta

List-II:
I. Fine branch of the renal artery that forms the glomerulus
II. U-shaped vessel running parallel to Henle's loop
III. Carries blood away from the glomerulus
IV. Fine capillary network around the renal tubule

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: The glomerulus is a tuft of capillaries formed by the afferent arteriole, a fine branch of the renal artery. Blood leaves it through the efferent arteriole, which forms the peritubular capillaries around the renal tubule. A minute vessel of this network runs parallel to Henle's loop as the U-shaped vasa recta.
steps: Vasa recta → U-shaped, parallel to Henle's loop (II)
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap the afferent and efferent arterioles, the peritubular network and vasa recta, or the efferent arteriole and the peritubular network.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Excretory Products and their Elimination', human excretory system: nephron
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-I, B-III, C-IV, D-II

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: Apart from increasing water reabsorption from the latter parts of the tubule, ADH can also increase the glomerular filtration rate. It does so by:

options.text: Dilating the afferent arteriole and lowering blood pressure
Constricting blood vessels, which raises blood pressure and thereby glomerular blood flow
Stimulating the atrial walls to release ANF

solution.explanation: NCERT: ADH can also affect kidney function through its constrictory effect on blood vessels. This raises blood pressure, and a rise in blood pressure can increase glomerular blood flow and thereby the GFR.
steps: ↑ blood pressure → ↑ glomerular blood flow → ↑ GFR
solution.why_others_wrong: A gives the opposite effect; renin, not ADH, converts angiotensinogen; ANF is released by the atria in response to increased blood flow, not by ADH.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Excretory Products and their Elimination', regulation of kidney function

Statement II: Sebaceous glands eliminate certain substances such as sterols, hydrocarbons and waxes through sebum.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: Sweat is a watery fluid with NaCl, small amounts of urea and lactic acid; its main function is cooling, but it also removes some wastes. Sebum from sebaceous glands eliminates sterols, hydrocarbons and waxes and gives the skin a protective oily covering. Both statements are true.
steps: Sebum removes sterols, hydrocarbons, waxes → II true

solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the counter-current mechanism in the human kidney are correct?

(a) The filtrate flows in opposite directions in the two limbs of Henle's loop.
(b) Blood flows through the two limbs of the vasa recta in a counter-current pattern.
(c) NaCl transported out by the ascending limb of Henle's loop is exchanged with the descending limb of the vasa recta.
(d) The mechanism maintains an osmolarity of the interstitium that increases towards the cortex.
(e) Small amounts of urea that enter the thin segment of the ascending limb are transported back to the interstitium by the collecting tubule.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Henle's loop and the vasa recta each carry flows in opposite directions in their two limbs. NaCl from the ascending limb of Henle's loop is exchanged with the descending limb of the vasa recta and returned to the interstitium by its ascending portion; urea is recycled from the thin ascending segment via the collecting tubule. Together these maintain an osmolarity that increases towards the inner medulla, not the cortex.
steps: (d) False: increases towards the inner medulla
solution.why_others_wrong: A and B include (d); D leaves out the true statement (b).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Excretory Products and their Elimination', mechanism of concentration of the filtrate

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In haemodialysis, blood drained from a convenient vein is pumped into the dialysing unit, and the cleared blood is returned to the body through an artery after adding anti-heparin.
Statement II: The dialysing fluid has the same composition as plasma, except for the nitrogenous wastes.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: In haemodialysis, blood is drained from a convenient artery, an anticoagulant such as heparin is added, and it is pumped into the dialysing unit; the cleared blood is pumped back through a vein after adding anti-heparin. Statement I reverses artery and vein, so it is false. The dialysing fluid matches plasma except that it lacks nitrogenous wastes, so these move out of the blood by concentration gradient (Statement II true).
steps: Drained from an artery, returned through a vein → I false
Dialysing fluid = plasma minus nitrogenous wastes → II true
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Excretory Products and their Elimination', disorders of the excretory system: haemodialysis
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: Which statement about the urine of a healthy adult human is correct?

options.text: It is slightly acidic (pH about 6.0), and on average 25–30 g of urea is excreted per day
It is slightly alkaline (pH about 8.0), and on average 25–30 g of urea is excreted per day
It is slightly acidic (pH about 6.0), and an adult excretes on average 5–6 L of it per day

solution.why_others_wrong: B denies the stated link; C and D call a true statement false.

questions.subject: Zoology

questions.subject: Zoology

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the cross-bridge cycle of muscle contraction are correct?

(a) After the power stroke, the myosin head releases ADP and Pi and goes back to its relaxed state.
(b) During contraction, the I-bands lengthen while the A-bands shorten.
(c) The cross bridge pulls the attached actin filaments towards the centre of the A-band.
(d) The Z-lines attached to the actin filaments are pulled inwards, shortening the sarcomere.
(e) Binding of a new ATP molecule to the myosin head breaks the cross bridge.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: The cross bridge pulls actin filaments towards the centre of the A-band; the Z-lines attached to them move inwards, so the sarcomere shortens. During shortening the I-bands get reduced while the A-bands retain their length. The myosin then releases ADP and Pi and returns to its relaxed state; a new ATP binds and the cross bridge is broken, and the cycle repeats.
steps: (b) False: I-bands shorten, A-bands keep their length
solution.why_others_wrong: B and C include (b); D leaves out the true statement (a).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Locomotion and Movement', mechanism of muscle contraction

questions.subject: Zoology

questions.subject: Zoology

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about a resting (polarised) axon are correct?

(a) The axoplasm contains a high concentration of K⁺ and negatively charged proteins and a low concentration of Na⁺.
(b) The fluid outside the axon contains a low concentration of K⁺ and a high concentration of Na⁺.
(c) The resting axonal membrane is impermeable to the negatively charged proteins present in the axoplasm.
(d) The ionic gradients across the resting membrane are maintained by passive diffusion alone, without any use of energy.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Ionic basis of the resting potential
solution.explanation: Inside the axon, K⁺ and negatively charged proteins are high and Na⁺ is low; outside, K⁺ is low and Na⁺ is high. The membrane is impermeable to the negatively charged proteins of the axoplasm. The ionic gradients are maintained by the active transport of ions by the sodium-potassium pump (3 Na⁺ out for 2 K⁺ in), which uses energy.
steps: (d) False: maintained by the Na⁺-K⁺ pump (active transport)
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and C include the false statement (d); A and B also leave out true statements.

Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

NCERT also states that the neural system of all animals is made of neurons that detect, receive and transmit different kinds of stimuli (Statement II true).

Neurons detect, receive, transmit stimuli → II true

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text: Site A on an axon has just been stimulated, and site B, immediately ahead of it, is still at rest. Which statement about the charges and the local current between the two sites is correct?

options.text: At A the inner surface is negative and at B it is positive; current flows on the inner surface from B to A
At A the inner surface is positive and at B it is negative; current flows on the inner surface from A to B and on the outer surface from B to A
At A the inner surface is positive and at B it is negative; current flows on both the inner and the outer surface from A to B
At A and at B the inner surface is positive; no current flows between them

solution.explanation: At the stimulated site A, Na⁺ influx reverses the polarity: the outer surface becomes negative and the inner surface positive. At site B, still at rest, the outer surface is positive and the inner negative. So current flows on the inner surface from A to B, and on the outer surface from B to A, completing the circuit. This depolarises B, and the impulse moves along the axon.
steps: Inner current A → B; outer current B → A
solution.why_others_wrong: A reverses the charges; C ignores that the circuit is completed in the opposite direction on the outer surface; D treats the resting site as depolarised.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Biology, 'Neural Control and Coordination', generation and conduction of nerve impulse
solution.final_answer: Option B: At A the inner surface is positive and at B it is negative; current flows on the inner surface from A to B and on the outer surface from B to A

questions.subject: Zoology

Non-nutrient chemicals that act as intercellular messengers and are produced in trace amounts
Enzymes poured by exocrine glands into ducts
Chemicals that act only inside the cell that produces them

solution.explanation: Hormones are non-nutrient chemicals which act as intercellular messengers and are produced in trace amounts. They are carried to target organs, which may be far from the gland that secretes them.

questions.subject: Zoology

questions.subject: Zoology
questions.question_text:

Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
